Title: IRS official who refused to testify facing more scrutiny over scandal, past

Title: White House Plays Down Data Program
Summary:
WASHINGTON — The Obama administration attempted to marshal new evidence in defense of its collection of private Internet and telephone data on Saturday, arguing that a secret program called Prism is simply an “internal government computer system” designed to sort through court-supervised collection of data, and that Congress has been briefed 13 times on the programs since 2009. After rushing to declassify some carefully selected descriptions of the programs, James R. Clapper Jr., the director of national intelligence, conceded for the first time that the Prism program existed. But in a statement, after denouncing the leak of the data to The Guardian and The Washington Post, Mr. Clapper insisted it was “not an undisclosed collection or data mining program.” Instead, he said it was a computer system to “facilitate” the collection of foreign intelligence that had been authorized by Congress. He appeared to be attempting to push back against early reports that the government had direct access to the huge computer servers at Google, Microsoft, Facebook and similar companies. Those firms have denied they give the government a “back door” to their systems.

A summary of a story is called an abstract. An abstract is a paragraph, no more than half a page long. You should always include your thesis statement in the summary, since you won't do any other summarizing unless you've got something specific to cite.
How To Write A Good Summary Of An Article?
Here are steps to write a summary of an article.
Step 1: Focus on the content
While doing the summary, you must understand the article well. Reading again and again will help you grasp the full picture.
Step 2: Make notes while reading the article
During the whole process of writing a good summary, make sure you take down important points. Making notes will help you keep track of things better.
Step 3: Prepare an outline
If possible, create a rough outline of how you want the information to appear in the paper. Then put the outline together into one document.
Step 4: Choose a summary type
There are two major types of article summaries - "narrative" and "descriptive". Both require careful planning ahead, but narratives tend to be much shorter than descriptives.
Step 5: Do the research
After you have prepared everything necessary, start looking up sources online. Find out what others say about these topics and try to incorporate their views into yours. This will give your readers valuable context on why you chose particular subjects for your paper.
What Does Abstract Mean?
An abstract is a short summary of your entire dissertation. You can think of it as a brief introduction to your work – like a teaser trailer for a movie!
Your professor may ask you to write an abstract before writing anything else. Or maybe he/she wants you to submit both the title page and the abstract at once. Either way, you need to prepare yourself properly because writing an abstract isn’t easy.
Abstracts usually contain between 200–300 words. They serve several purposes:
· Give readers a sense of what kind of paper they’re going to read. If the author fails to give enough detail here, chances are they’ll lose interest before getting past the second paragraph.
· Help readers decide whether or not they’re interested in continuing to read further. If someone reads the abstract and thinks “meh”, then there’s really nothing else to see anyway. That saves everyone time.

WASHINGTON -– Today, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the National Credit Union Administration (collectively the Agencies) issued a joint statement regarding the effect of the Supreme Court decision in United States v. Windsor, which struck down part of the Defense of Marriage Act, on the bank regulatory capital rules. Specifically, the Agencies will accept the supervisory capital treatment of an institution’s investment in its subsidiaries under the Basel III international capital standards until December 31, 2014. See 77 Fed. Reg. 44940 (July 26, 2012). Title: I.R.S. Official Invokes 5th Amendment at Hearing
Summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Former IRS official Lois G. Lerner invoked her constitutional right against self-incrimination Wednesday, defying a congressional demand that she explain her role in the agency's political targeting of tea party groups seeking tax-exempt status. After Lerner testified before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, panel Chairman Darrell Issa, R-Calif., warned that she might face legal action if she does not appear before the full House next month. "The consequences of her invocation of the Fifth Amendment privilege cannot be ignored," Issa said. Lerner, head of the Exempt Organizations unit in the IRS, came under fire earlier this year when IRS officials acknowledged that they had unfairly targeted tea party groups because of their politics. Lerner apologized for the practice and resigned effective Monday. She testified behind closed doors at the Capitol on Tuesday, and her comments became public when the panel released its transcript. In prepared remarks, Lerner described her anger over learning about the practice late last year, telling lawmakers that "it was an error and it should never have happened." In addition to denouncing such conduct, she said she had recommended that criminal investigations begin immediately and that all involved be held accountable.

Title: Obama Defends NSA Programs, Says Congress Knew About Surveillance
Summary:
This story should be summarized in an unbiased way that captures the main elements of the story without any sort of partisan bent. The lead should highlight the fact that a president of the United States is actively defending government surveillance programs that he authorizes.
In a pair of major speeches this week, President Barack Obama forcefully defended revelations that the National Security Agency is collecting phone records and electronic communications, saying that Congress was fully briefed and the programs are limited in scope. Obama’s speech on NSA surveillance was delivered Tuesday night before the annual dinner of the American Constitution Society, a legal group founded by progressive Democratic activists. He repeated much of what he said to reporters the previous afternoon outside a Walmart in Maryland.
Obama said his administration will no longer “collect signals intelligence against leaders of friendly nations” if they have provided information deemed useful. He added that all Americans’ metadata — which includes location data about mobile phones, tablets and computers — will now only be collected for one year rather than two years previously. After that time period, the records must be destroyed unless there is another foreign policy or counterterrorism purpose, he said. Additionally, the NSA will now have to seek permission from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to query Americans’ phone records, rather than being able to do so without approval.
Obama also announced that the director of national intelligence would create a new task force of senior officials “to report directly to me on our efforts to address technological changes.” That task force will include the secretaries of State, Defense, Homeland Security and Energy; Attorney General Eric Holder; Director of National Intelligence James Clapper; and White House Chief of Staff Denis McDonough.
“We’re going to continue to reform programs and draw lines,” Obama said. He said he would hold agencies accountable to the public about their policies for collecting information through a new set of rules that would govern their sharing of information among various branches of the federal government. Those rules, he said, would prohibit such transfers of information unless they are legally permissible, necessary to protect life, critical to national security or otherwise lawful.

Obama said Thursday his administration will work to reform provisions in the Patriot Act that allowed for the NSA to collect massive quantities of phone metadata in a single database.

After years of bipartisan opposition to raising the debt limit, the White House announced last week that President Obama supports raising it without any strings attached. The announcement has sparked immediate outrage from conservatives who say they will not vote to raise the debt ceiling again, but they're also drawing praise from liberals who say Republicans won't hold the president hostage on the issue again like they did two years ago.
Conservative Rep. Tim Huelskamp (R-Kan.) was one of several members of Congress who criticized Obama for his support of an increase in the nation's borrowing cap without concessions from Democrats to reduce spending and cut the national debt.
His statement comes after Obama broke with tradition by calling on Congress to suspend the debt limit without any strings attached. Republicans have been critical of the move since it means no debate on reducing the national debt or increasing revenues. However, the House Democratic Steering Committee Chairman is pushing back against that sentiment by arguing that the debt ceiling shouldn’t be used as a political football anymore.
Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas), chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, says there should be a requirement to suspend the debt ceiling for fiscal 2014. It's the latest example of how Republicans are using their newfound power as the majority party in the U.S. House of Representatives to drive the agenda forward, rather than waiting around for Democrats or Obama to act first.
"If Congress does nothing else, then let us do one thing. Let's restore fiscal discipline and accountability in Washington," he wrote in an op-ed published Friday in Roll Call. He continued: "While we are passing bills, it is time to pass some bills that actually affect our economy and our people in real ways — not just words. That begins with restoring the separation between legislating and appropriating funds. ... [W]e must stop throwing money at problems that simply don't exist in the first place. A new study finds that people can change their behavior when given information about how others are behaving.
People are social animals; research has shown that they will mimic what they see others doing. Now scientists have found that merely telling people about the habits and health status of those around them can cause individuals to change their own behavior. In addition, when people learned that their community was engaging in risky behavior, they were able to alter that behavior.
Researchers from Carnegie Mellon University, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston Medical Center and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health set out to determine whether providing community members with information about the habits and health conditions of their neighbors could encourage positive changes in individual behavior. They designed a multiyear trial involving 18 neighborhoods across Baltimore City during a period that coincided with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's 2010 Community Health Assessment.
Participants received letters each quarter stating such facts as how many smokers, diabetes patients, hypertensive people, stroke victims and pregnant women lived within their neighborhoods. They also learned how many people in their neighborhoods were physically active and obese. Each participant also received a letter listing his or her personal risk factors, including whether he or she was a current smoker, obese or engaged in regular physical activity.
After one year, participants who received the letters were more likely to receive cancer screenings and less likely to smoke, while the communities surrounding them reported fewer hospital visits and emergency room admissions due to heart attacks and strokes. People living in the areas surrounding the community groups saw fewer days off work and reduced absences among children.

Congressman Raul Labrador of Idaho, one of 38 House Republicans who voted against the budget agreement last month, said today that he intends to run for majority leader on Thursday.
If elected, Labrador would have his hands full immediately dealing with House Republicans who believe that deficits should not exist at all and others who say the federal debt is now at crisis levels that require some action.

He came under intense pressure at the time from House Republican leaders, but stuck to his principles — saying in a letter to colleagues that the measure was “an example of Washington politics as usual.”

House Oversight Chairman Jason Chaffetz, R-Utah, demanded last week that the State Department turn over any and all emails sent by Clinton while she was serving as secretary of state under President Barack Obama from Jan. 21, 2009, until Feb. 1, 2013.
Chaffetz, who also serves as the ranking member on the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, said he wanted all such communications turned over so that the committees could determine whether they contained classified material, including information deemed “top secret/sensitive compartmentalized information.”
Chaffetz also demanded that the department identify every person who received copies of the emails, as well as every copy and draft that exists of the messages.
He specifically demanded the release of any correspondence marked classified or containing classified information that includes the now infamous term, “FOIA.” Such an item is often referred to as FOIA — the Freedom of Information Act.
“As the Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, I am concerned about the possibility of the improper handling of classified materials on a system which you controlled solely as Secretary of State,” Chaffetz wrote. “It is therefore imperative that the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Select Committee on Benghazi review these records to ensure they complied with federal recordkeeping requirements and that there is no evidence of intentional mishandling of classified information.”
Chaffetz added that he hoped the State Department would be able to assist his inquiry by Thursday.
The Utah representative called the incident “unacceptable” and told Fox News on Friday that Congress needed to find out how it happened. He reiterated that statement on Tuesday.
“I want to make sure that we have transparency,” he said. “We don’t know anything yet. We really don’t. The State Department has told us nothing … we just need to make sure everything is above board and transparent here.”
Chaffetz questioned why the State Department waited several weeks to inform Congress of Clinton’s apparent mishandling of classified information.

The Obama administration's new student loan rules will benefit millions of Americans, a White House official says.
White House officials are downplaying conservative criticism that students are going to face tighter credit restrictions under new Department of Education regulations governing private student lending companies.
While borrowers with less than stellar academic backgrounds or financial history may see their lenders get stingier, that doesn't mean they won't have access to funds, a senior White House economic adviser argued Tuesday on MSNBC's "Morning Joe."
"This will lead to better terms and conditions for consumers than what's currently out there," Jason Furman, a deputy assistant secretary for Economic Policy at the Office of Management and Budget, said when asked why the administration didn't just ban private lending altogether.
"But there might be some cases where you need to have some sort of ability to choose between different options," he added.
Under the new rules, which are designed to protect students by requiring lenders to verify a borrower's expected income at least three times over five years, colleges and universities can no longer offer their own aid packages to students without the same scrutiny.
The changes require private lenders to show how much money students will be earning in the future — "which makes sense," according to Furman.
But conservatives see it differently, criticizing the administration for restricting lending options and limiting access to capital for those who need it most.
"What's being done here is really punishing certain types of students that have low expectations and therefore will never graduate college," Rep. John Kline, R-Minn., chairman of the House Education and Labor Committee told Bloomberg Businessweek.
Education Secretary Arne Duncan shot back Monday in an op-ed in Politico, calling the critics "completely wrong," saying that students will still have plenty of lending options once they graduate.
"They can look for the lowest rates available and choose among many reputable lenders," he wrote. "Moreover, these changes will make the system stronger -- giving borrowers more choices among trustworthy lenders and strengthening the institutions that provide these critical loans."

The subject line of the email read: “$10,000 for every word of this RNC speech?!”
In the body of the email, the Democratic party warned its supporters about what it claimed was a wasteful spending pattern among Republican lawmakers, who, it alleges, are willing to spend any amount of taxpayer dollars needed to secure a partisan advantage for themselves or their allies.

In comparison, the DNC says Democrats will spend only $2.6 million per day during their convention. The DNC also notes that Republicans will reportedly use up 80 percent of the $40 million total allocated to the four political parties in advance of the conventions — while Democrats, in contrast, will use less than half that sum.
However, the Democrats' email ignores the fact that Republicans plan to hold their convention over seven days while Democrats intend to stage theirs over four days — a factor which would seemingly increase the actual cost per day for both sides (the two parties' respective conventions will be held simultaneously).
Aside from the fact that the $5 million figure represents a cost per day of roughly $750,000 — not $10,000 — the DNC fails to note that it has no idea how much Republicans intend to spend for their convention overall; it just assumes that they will spend more than Democrats, based on the amount already designated for each side.
Beyond this, Democrats fail to consider the possibility that they may wind up exceeding their self-imposed limit because their convention runs longer than planned, as has happened before in other election years.

Summary:

House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) and President Barack Obama met at the White House on Thursday night to discuss how to avert the nation’s so-called “fiscal cliff” – the series of automatic spending cuts and tax increases set to begin Jan. 2 unless Congress acts to delay them.
Observers were divided on whether the encounter would produce meaningful progress in negotiations aimed at preventing the worst effects of an economy-rattling budget crisis. But they all agreed that the two men probably won’t tell the media what happened in their roughly one-hour meeting.
Neither side released any statement following the get-together. But House Republicans didn’t seem too enthusiastic about the idea of their leader disclosing details about what happened during the closed-door session.
“You’ll never hear me discuss it,” Rep. Tom Cole (R-Okla.), who represents the district where the summit took place, told msnbc’s Chuck Todd.
Republican leaders sent a similar message when asked if they were worried that a lack of transparency could fuel doubts among Americans over whether there really was progress.
“I don’t think we should discuss these negotiations,” said Rep. Lynn Jenkins (R-Kansas), who sits on the budget committee. “We haven’t done that historically and I don’t want to start doing it now.”
Rep. Matt Salmon (R-Ariz.) added that he wasn’t concerned because “they know us well enough” that they shouldn’t release too many details about the talks.
“They’ve seen the cards,” he said. “We’ve got nothing left to hide.”

After more than 50 minutes of conversation, the talks between President Barack Obama and House Speaker John Boehner broke off in mid-sentence late Thursday afternoon. That left it to Vice President Joe Biden and Treasury Secretary Tim Geithner to continue the session. And so, as the sun set on Washington, the most high profile meeting yet in the fiscal-cliff standoff remained unresolved.
White House officials said Mr. Boehner's chief of staff, Michael Sommers, and senior policy adviser Brett Loper joined him in the session. Mr. Obama was accompanied only by the director of his legislative affairs office, Rob Nabors.
For now, however, Mr. Obama and Mr. Boehner seemed determined not to let the meeting go down in history as another disappointment. The White House quickly released a joint statement saying they would resume discussions Saturday—an optimistic sign given that both men have often portrayed themselves as unable to get through a day without talking to each other.
"The meeting was productive, and we agreed that our staff should follow-up on the issues we discussed today," the statement said. "In addition, the President invited the Speaker to come to the White House again before year's end for the purpose of continuing these conversations."
Indeed, Mr. Obama's decision to schedule such a high-profile encounter at the height of the holiday season indicates just how important he views reaching a budget deal with Republicans.
"Everyone knows I want to get this done by Christmas if possible," the President said in brief remarks at the White House on Friday morning, adding that he was confident they could reach an agreement.
Mr. Boehner didn't seem to share those sentiments. "There are still significant differences remaining," the Ohio Republican said following his meeting with the President. "I don't think we're going to solve these problems before the New Year. We'll keep working on them."

Title: Sparks fly as Biden, Ryan face off in feisty vice presidential debate
Summary:
In a head-to-head battle of proxies, Vice President Joe Biden wasted no time Thursday trying to do what many Democrats felt President Barack Obama failed to against Republican nominee Mitt Romney – going on offense with an often disdainful attack on Rep. Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) – who stood his ground against a barrage of Biden grins, guffaws, snickers and interruptions.
The dueling running mates turned the lone vice presidential debate into an uncharacteristically feisty affair, scrapping over everything from the economy to Libya to taxes. But it was the vice president who set the aggressive tone, blatantly striving to hit the reset button after President Obama was panned for his lackluster performance at last week’s opening debate.
If Obama was too cold, Biden at times bordered on too hot, analysts said afterward.
Biden chuckled and smirked through many of Ryan’s responses. But unlike Obama a week ago, he let few points go unchallenged.
He chided Ryan about the latter’s own record, saying: “You can’t tell it straight in a straight line.”
Ryan shot back, in reference to Biden’s tendency to make gaffes: “As the vice president very well knows … sometimes the words don’t come out of your mouth the right way.”
“I always say what I mean,” Biden responded.
Notably, Biden hammered Romney over his secretly videotaped comment in which he said he doesn’t have to worry about the “47 percent” of Americans who don’t pay federal income taxes.
The vice president’s remark, though, prompted some Republicans to wonder whether he’s truly ready to take the reins should tragedy strike the Obama White House.

Title: Sparks fly as Biden, Ryan face off in feisty vice presidential debate
Summary:
A debate about competing visions for America’s future, and about the character of the men themselves. Biden played the part of “good cop” while Ryan played “bad cop,” and each tried to frame the other as a caricature rather than a full person. Both men are highly intelligent; Ryan demonstrated a depth of knowledge and understanding of complex problems and solutions that was somewhat shocking (for example, he clearly understood the nuances of the Affordable Care Act – even though he hates it). That said, neither man provided much evidence of deep thought outside of memorized talking points.
The debate was more about character, personalities and temperaments. It was easy to see the differences between Ryan and Biden based upon their body language and general air of confidence. Ryan was assertive, confident and generally positive in his outlook. Biden appeared overconfident and smug, and even a bit condescending towards Ryan. This gave him an impression that he is dismissive of other views, unwilling to learn, and arrogant in his position. If he comes off that way in person, he probably does in private meetings as well.
Neither Ryan nor Biden articulated or defended his vision for America. Both men focused on attacks against their opponents, and they spent far more time trying to diminish their opponents then presenting their own ideas. As such, the debate was an argument about character rather than substance.

Obama administration plans to release nearly 10 billion gallons of treated but still toxic water from the reservoir behind the country's largest dam into Lake Michigan each summer, a move that would expose millions of people downstream to a host of health problems, including cancer, according to a report released Wednesday by environmental advocacy groups.
"Once you look at the magnitude of what we're talking about, it is staggering," said Katherine McCarty, director of government affairs for the Environmental Law and Policy Center (ELPC), which released the study. "It changes everything."
Nearly all of the water that flows through the Great Lakes begins in Minnesota and Wisconsin before heading south through Chicago and eventually emptying into the Gulf of Mexico. Under the agreement between Illinois and Indiana, 85 percent of the runoff draining from northern Illinois farmland is pumped northward into Lake Michigan. That volume swells to 98 percent during years when heavy rain falls.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers estimates that 637 million gallons of contaminated runoff pour into Lake Michigan each year. The latest science shows that much of that water is carrying pollutants that could harm human health and wildlife populations, the ELPC said. In its report, titled "Downstream Damage," the group listed a dozen health threats it says come from agricultural chemicals, fertilizers and manure that drain into the lake.
The ELPC asked state officials to conduct an immediate review of agricultural practices in Illinois and Wisconsin. It also recommended imposing penalties on cities and towns in those two states that discharge too much contamination into local streams and rivers.
Illinois Farm Bureau spokeswoman Carol Bender said she believes the state's farmers use the best technology available to prevent soil erosion. But she noted that the federal government's agricultural conservation program doesn't require farmers to prove their best practices were followed.
"We continue to work with the federal government to develop programs whereby producers would receive incentives and technical assistance to help them adopt Best Management Practices or even more advanced management practices," Bender said.
The Indiana Department of Environmental Management didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Romney campaign officials sought to portray Ryan as a more honest broker of entitlement reform than their former presidential candidate, Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.). Democrats and liberal bloggers countered that Ryan's plans are no less draconian than those of McCain and former Gov. Sarah Palin (R) of Alaska.
"You don't have to worry about any age group," Ryan said in the fallout from his selection as Romney's vice-presidential nominee, appearing on "Fox News Sunday." He added that "every American family knows how to live within its means."

"I think he ought to talk to some families where both parents work, and see if he thinks they can live within their means. I think he needs to go down to Texas and look at what's happening there and see if it sounds like living within one's means."
Schumer's remark referred to the fact that Ryan wants to convert Medicaid into a system of capped federal grants to states, whose governors would then decide how to distribute aid. Ryan's plan, however, has received a mixed reception among conservatives. It does not affect the number of people who receive Medicaid, nor does it necessarily make deep cuts. Instead, it would give governors greater flexibility in allocating resources.
Paul Krugman wrote in his New York Times column that "Mr. Ryan's plan to turn Medicaid into a block grant might actually mean higher spending, because the states wouldn't have to spend as much as they do now; they could just say no when poor people showed up at the door."
Ryan's choice was almost instantly seized upon by Democrats to frame the debate around Medicare. The program serves as a central issue in the election, especially given recent Republican attacks on the popular retirement benefit.

Summary:
The VP debates have been going on since Reagan-Mondale and are little more than political theater. The media takes them too seriously. In reality, they have almost zero impact on the election. The people who watch these things usually already know how they're going to vote. People who change their minds based on these debates are rare and usually not good news for the incumbent party (it means they can now see through its rhetoric).
Both parties' presumptive nominees have high negatives among voters; that's why we get a third party candidate in the race at least half the time - someone whom voters can imagine voting for while still being able to support either major party nominee if push comes to shove.
Even though he is a bit of a lightweight and doesn't really have much of a chance, libertarian congressman Ron Paul has more support than any other third party candidate. That makes sense given that libertarians are mostly Republicans who would rather their party nominate someone like Paul instead of an establishment GOP hack or a crazy conservative Democrat. It's not clear whether enough Democrats feel this way to make a difference, but I suspect there must be some because we haven't seen a third party spoiler since Perot ran in '92. If there is a large number of libertarian-leaning Democratic voters, maybe the LP will start fielding stronger candidates. It could also mean that Paul's base is made up mostly of Democrats who lean libertarian.
Libertarian Congressman Bob Barr, who lost his bid for reelection in '02 to Rep. Cynthia McKinney (D), probably had lots of these kind of Democratic votes in '08 when he ran against McConnell. But he won just 1% of the national popular vote while Paul took 13%. While Barr didn't run a third party candidacy in '08, the fact that he had more Democratic votes than Paul indicates there are more than enough Democratic voters sympathetic toward libertarian ideas.
As for the other Republicans in the race - Huckabee, Romney, Giuliani - there's a strong possibility that none of them can win the nomination without having to compromise on core principles. This is why I keep saying that they may go down fighting between themselves.

The White House says Mr. Obama is meeting with House Republicans at 1 p.m. EST Tuesday. Aides say the meeting will last around 90 minutes.

On Sunday, House Majority Leader Eric Cantor said there is no agreement yet between the White House and congressional leaders on how best to close loopholes.
Mr. Obama is encouraging lawmakers to act swiftly to avert higher taxes. Both he and Vice President Joe Biden have made clear that they aren't prepared to make concessions aimed at appeasing Republicans on issues that aren't central to the impasse over tax policy.
Republican lawmakers say they'd rather wait out the deadline than accept a package that includes raising tax rates for high earners.

A group of researchers have developed a novel way to measure lung capacity in young children -- a technique they say could help identify infected children faster, ultimately saving lives.
A team of Australian medical experts have created a new screening tool for pneumonia (lung infection) in infectious diseases clinics and hospitals. Called the Pneumonia Work Index (PWI), the test provides a simple way to measure a child's lung capacity before and after a course of antibiotics. If the child's breathing improves after treatment then he/she may not need to go through a range of costly investigations. But if there isn't any improvement, doctors can move quickly to investigate further and prescribe appropriate treatments.
"Children admitted to hospital with severe illness caused by pneumonia often undergo multiple tests and procedures when sometimes none are necessary," says Dr Linda de Swart, a Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne paediatrician who led the development of the PWI. "In many cases these tests provide no benefit to patients."
Dr de Swart conducted the research while at the Murdoch Childrens Research Institute and The Royal Children's Hospital along with colleagues from across Australia. The work, published today in PLOS ONE, is supported by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia.
She says the current guidelines for diagnosing pneumonia include things like chest X-rays, blood tests and cultures, but don't take into account how well the patient is doing. The PWI measures vital signs and heart rate, and assesses the level of sickness, anxiety and activity of the child before and after taking antibiotics. The results show whether treatment has been successful and whether further investigation is needed.
"This means we won't keep children in hospital unnecessarily and we won't waste valuable resources. Instead we can focus our limited resources where they're most needed, on children whose condition hasn't improved," says Dr de Swart.
Further work is needed before the PWI can be rolled out to general use.

Credit: Lonny Giacchetta. Source: University of Southern California.
Intermittent fasting – or not eating food for a set amount of time – is increasingly popular among dieters, especially those trying to lose weight quickly. But scientists aren’t sure exactly how the practice works. Now, a team of researchers from the University of Southern California says they may have found out. They published their findings on March 14 in Nature Communications.
For the study, the researchers collected data from the brains and skeletal muscles of mice. They discovered that short periods of intermittent fasting trigger the regrowth of stem cells in damaged organs. This process, known as autophagy, has been shown to reduce inflammation and disease risk in obese individuals. However, most studies conducted thus far used live animals to simulate human health.
“While mice have proven valuable in understanding diseases, their genetic differences make translating results to humans difficult,” said lead author Valter Longo, director of USC’s Longevity Institute. “In contrast, human skin and gut tissue share similarities with those of mice, providing a much more realistic testing ground for our research.”
Longo and his colleagues also discovered that short bouts of fasting may spur healthy tissue growth within certain regions of the body, while other areas could experience negative effects. As a result, future autophagy research will need to take location into consideration when planning experiments.
“As we age, every organ in our body begins to deteriorate,” added study senior author Benjamin Bikman, assistant professor of gerontology and biological sciences at USC Davis School of Gerontology. “Because aging and obesity are risk factors for almost every chronic disease, it is essential that we understand the processes of aging and obesity at a molecular level if we hope to develop therapies to treat and prevent these conditions.”

Republicans have enough votes to overcome such a move, and doing so would also allow them to force through other key items on their agenda without Democratic obstruction.
While the nuclear option has been used several times before in the history of the Senate, no sitting senator has ever voted for or against it, according to CQ Roll Call. The last time it was done involved changing the rules of the Senate to make it easier to eliminate the filibuster altogether (though that hasn’t happened).
The nuclear option, which was introduced in the early days of the country, would allow a simple majority of the Senate (usually a bare minimum of 50 out of 100) to pass major bills. Currently, any bill needs the support of three-fifths of the Senate, usually a supermajority of 60 senators. However, there are currently 52 Republicans in the Senate and 48 Democrats, meaning that Republicans already possess this number of votes to approve most legislation without needing Democratic support.

Title: Reid: Mosque Should Be Built Someplace Else

On Tuesday, September 21st, Sen. The senator’s comment marked the second time since Obama announced support for the mosque that a member of Congress publicly opposed the idea of constructing the building on such hallowed ground. Previously, Rep. Peter King (R-NY), one of the few congressmen to openly express displeasure at the notion of constructing the mosque, said he “will try his best to prevent them” from doing so.

Although many onlookers believe that both the GOP and Democrats will ultimately seek to avoid the hot-button political topic altogether, the fact remains that Reid’s reversal makes clear that there is still a great deal of debate within the body politic over how best to handle the situation in New York.
Few, if any, major developments occurred between the conclusion of Reid’s statement and publication of this summary. As such, it is difficult to determine what effect the senator’s reversal may have had upon the course of events in New York; however, given the gravity of the decision and the potential backlash that Reid could receive from his constituency and other Democratic Party members alike, it is safe to assume that he weighed every option available before making his final proclamation.
In essence, Reid’s decision marks another chapter in what has been an ongoing saga in American politics. It is likely that further debates and discussions will continue until either another resolution is reached or the matter comes to a close. Either way, it appears as though neither side has given up on the fight – even if it means taking a hit in terms of public opinion along the way.

After a New York Times report, Rep. Bob Filner, D-CA, may be facing a serious challenge to his re-election bid from Carl DeMaio, the chief financial officer for San Diego City Councilman Brian Bilbray.
Carl DeMaio, the city councilman from San Diego’s 5th district, announced Monday that he is forming a committee to explore a run against Democrat Rep. Bob Filner in California's 51st congressional district.
“It’s my intent to give the voters a choice,” DeMaio told the Union Tribune of San Diego. “There are many issues in the House of Representatives where Democrats and Republicans differ greatly. I want to provide those options to the voters.”
Filner (D), who won office in November, defeated his Republican opponent, 5th district business owner Peter Jacobi, by nearly 30 percentage points.
DeMaio has been an outspoken critic of the local pension system, saying it needs reform so as to avoid bankrupting the city. He is also openly gay, which could prove problematic if he wins the nomination.
His potential candidacy caught local reporters off guard because he hadn't before publically stated he would run. But some speculate that the fact that he hasn't filed any campaign finance reports yet indicates that he might still pull back from the race.
If he does remain a candidate, he faces a tough battle, as the 51st includes cities such as Chula Vista, Imperial Beach, National City, Poway, Santee and Solana Beach -- all bastions of conservatism in the Southern California area. If he were to beat Filner in the election, the seat would become one of the most Republican districts in California.
But DeMaio has proved he can overcome big odds before. In 2006, he lost his bid for San Diego mayor but managed to garner over 44 percent of the vote, and he only lost by 5 percentage points in his district. That's despite a reputation as a hardline Republican who supports free enterprise and fiscal responsibility.

Title: Richard Blumenthal Calls NYT Report 'Outrageous Distortion'
Summary:
We are reporting that a recent New York Times story reported that Attorney General Richard Blumenthal has misled voters in Connecticut with regards to his participation in the Vietnam War.
Facts: After a New York Times review of his public statements, Blumenthal was found to have misrepresented himself in speeches and in an interview. He falsely claimed that he fought in Vietnam when, in fact, he was a captain in the Marines while serving stateside.
Analysis: The NYT’s findings are consistent with the information provided on Blumenthal’s official biography on his Senate webpage (http://blumenthalsenate.com/bio/). His biography indicates that he “served” in the Marines from 1970 through 1976. However, Blumenthal also indicates that he “entered service” upon his enlisting in 1970, indicating that he did not actually see combat duty until after entering military service, a point disputed by the NYT. In addition, Blumenthal also claims that he served as a Marine prosecutor in Vietnam despite his lack of such duty. The NYT claims that Blumenthal used “military jargon” (such as “took direct fire”) in his speeches without properly explaining it to his audience.
Bottom line: This case is more or less moot. While the NYT reports that Blumenthal deliberately mislead his constituents, the evidence seems unclear given the details provided on the AG’s Senate webpage. Furthermore, Blumenthal corrected himself by stating his real background to a crowd of veterans who confronted him.

Playing "This Land Is Your Land"
As students enter the classroom they should find a copy of "This Land Is Your Land," written by Woody Guthrie, posted at every table. Each student should be assigned to one of the tables and should receive a copy of the lyrics. When class begins, the teacher should read the entire song aloud while the students follow along on paper. Afterward, the teacher should ask students to reflect on the following:
What does the first verse of the song say?
When listening to the song, what images come to mind? Why?
Who sings the song? How old was she when she sang it?
Did you know that the song "This Land Is Your Land" was originally called "God Blessed America?" Did you know that Woody Guthrie changed the title after learning that Irving Berlin had previously registered it with ASCAP?
After listening to the song, the teacher can play it again so that students can hear the original version and compare it to the version we all learned growing up.
In pairs, students should create a short skit depicting the events described in "This Land Is Your Land." They could use flash cards, make props or costumes, etc., to bring the story alive. This activity could work well as a drama assignment.
For homework, assign students to write a short essay describing how living conditions have improved since the song was written.

Title: NAACP Resolution Calls on Tea Party to Repudiate 'Racist Elements' in Movement
Summary:
The NAACP adopted a resolution today condemning "racist elements" in the Tea Party movement and calling on the movement's leaders to repudiate bigotry, despite claims from Tea Partiers that the measure is just a political ploy.
The nation's leading civil rights group took up the language at its annual convention in Kansas City, MO. The resolution initially said the NAACP would "repudiate the racism of the Tea Parties" and stand against the movement's attempt to "push our country back to the pre-civil rights era," though the wording was amended to downplay criticism of all Tea Partiers while asking them to repudiate bigots in their own ranks.
NAACP leaders have referenced an incident in March when Tea Party protesters allegedly hurled racial epithets at black lawmakers on Capitol Hill ahead of a health care vote. But Tea Party members have challenged claims that their activists accosted black lawmakers in March and no visual evidence has been produced depicting a racist attack. Dallas Tea Party founder Phillip Dennis said "there was no proof" of racist behavior at the event and that the movement welcomed minority members.

A summary can be considered an abstract. An abstract should summarize or condense a work.
An abstract can present the main results found in the research paper. Abstracts are typically one paragraph long (see below). The purpose of the abstract is to give readers an understanding of what the entire research study is about, so they know if they want to read further. This will also help reviewers determine if your article is suitable for their journal and will save time by allowing them to decide to pass without reading the full text.
Abstract should consist of 150-200 words.
Abstract should include background information, methodology, findings, results & conclusion.
Abstract should not be structured around separate headings & subheadings.
Abstract should be written as a continuous block of text without any numbered items within it such as tables, figures or references.
Write your abstract at the end of your paper after you have finished writing the whole manuscript. You cannot write your abstract first before writing the rest of the paper. Remember, your abstract is a brief summary of your paper. Therefore, do not write it in advance.
How To Write Your Abstract?
You should use simple language in writing your abstract. Remember that your target reader might be from another discipline or from a different cultural background.
Start with a broad sentence stating the aim of your research. This usually follows a short introduction about the field of study where your research belongs. Mention key words or phrases related to your research topic. Do not forget to indicate the major findings and conclusions drawn from the results section.
When citations are included in an abstract, the citation style should follow the format used in the rest of the paper. Citing sources enhances the credibility of the author’s research. Make sure that the citations appear in square brackets [ ] and include relevant pages numbers. The citations must follow the bibliography format of the final reference list at the end of the paper.
If you include a table in your abstract, the table caption must follow the format provided in the paper. If you include a figure/photo or other graphics in the abstract, you must attach its title, source, and captions in parentheses immediately after the graphic. You can provide the references in the same way as the bibliography part of the rest of the paper.

Investors are now bidding up U.S. government debt. That's a huge problem.
This time it's different!
That's what many investors believed when they jumped back into risky assets last month. But it wasn't different.
It was business as usual. The same old game - speculative fever grips investors. They believe central bankers can do something to put off the reckoning. So they pile in. This time it's not the subprime mortgage market or real estate or collateralized debt obligations or corporate junk bonds. It's Treasuries.
U.S. government paper became the new "it" trade last month. Buyers are convinced the Federal Reserve can keep pushing down interest rates and printing money forever.
And the Fed is doing its part. Having promised not to raise rates until mid-2015, the central bank has made clear it won't even begin selling Treasury holdings. And it'll continue buying $40 billion worth each month through September. As long as there are buyers willing to pay more than the auction clears (the amount accepted at the lowest yield), the Fed will take the cash.
And that means the U.S. government is able to borrow money at rock-bottom prices... for the rest of time. Or so they say.
Here's why I don't see it that way.
Central banks are only creating more leverage. When the music stops, the losses could be catastrophic.
Treasurys have been the place to be for more than two years, says Michael Panzner, author of Financial Armageddon.
"They began to look like the safest possible asset class," he says. "Everybody wanted them."
Now investors think "there's nothing wrong with owning bills," he explains. "All the smart people own these bonds. Maybe we should too."
This isn't your grandmother's Treasury. In the past, the U.S. government sold short-, intermediate-, and long-term securities. Nowadays, it issues a single security called TIPS (Treasury Inflation Protected Securities). These bonds adjust their principal value with the rate of inflation.

In the United States, an individual who dies without leaving behind a will is deemed to have died “intestate.” Therefore, according to state laws governing property distribution upon death, the deceased person’s assets will be distributed among certain heirs, as specified under state law.
There are many types of laws regarding inheritance. In most states, intestacy rules determine how estate assets are distributed if no will exists at the time of someone’s death. Each U.S. state has its own rules concerning who inherits assets when there is no will, although spouses typically receive the largest share of the estate. Depending on the type of asset involved, the decedent’s children may inherit the entire estate. Assets will also pass to surviving parents and siblings. However, there are limits on who can inherit, such as blood relatives only, and the order of priority varies by state. Certain states also allow nonblood relatives to inherit, while other states place no limit on who can inherit what kind of asset.
In general, the first step in the process of determining how assets are distributed if no will exists at the time of death is to determine whether probate should occur, and in what form. Probate occurs once the court reviews the details of the case to see if everything appears legitimate. After this review, the will gets admitted into evidence, and the court decides whether the contents of the will are valid based on various legal criteria. If it is determined that the will is invalid, the estate then passes through probate using the provisions of intestacy laws. Even though assets often go through the probate process after the death of their owner, not every dollar will end up going through probate. There are plenty of assets that do not have to go through the probate process.
If the deceased had no living spouse or descendants at the time of his or her death, the assets will go to parents or siblings, depending on the state. As states continue to transition to remote learning, working, and governing models, adversaries have leveraged their cyber capabilities to target our nation’s weakest links: individuals. As such, the pandemic has served as a wakeup call about the pervasiveness of cyber threats—particularly ransomware—and how devastating these attacks can be.
As we enter the holiday season, IC leaders are reminding Americans to remain vigilant against social engineering tactics. Social engineering attacks leverage human nature and motivation as hackers attempt to trick individuals into giving away sensitive data or credentials. These attacks are prevalent across the private sector and often involve email phishing schemes and voice or video calls. In addition to deploying layered security approaches, IC recommends implementing multifactor authentication (MFA) and training employees on recognizing potential threats.

Title: Trump Declares National Emergency To Fund U.S.-Mexico Border Wall
Summary:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he would invoke his powers under the Constitution to secure additional funding for his promised border wall, marking a dramatic escalation in his fight to get the barrier built despite Congress’ refusal to provide the full $5.7 billion in taxpayer dollars that he wants.
Analysis: Mr. Trump’s plan to override Congress comes after he was unable to sway lawmakers toward his position during the longest government shutdown in United States history. At issue is the $5.7 billion Mr. Trump has requested for construction of a wall along the border with Mexico. After failing to persuade lawmakers to agree on the funding, Mr. Trump had threatened to declare a national emergency to obtain the money. But lawmakers appear to have reached a deal to end the shutdown, with Mr. Trump scheduled to deliver remarks on border security from the White House on Tuesday afternoon.
Mr. Trump’s announcement is likely to draw a swift response from Democrats. As of early Tuesday morning, there was little information about how Democratic leaders planned to handle the declaration, though Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader, wrote on Twitter that “no one should question our resolve to win this battle.” On Monday, Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, who helped negotiate a deal to reopen the government, said he thought a majority of senators would support the national emergency declaration if Mr. Trump made it.
At least 12 state attorneys general — including representatives of states near the border and those whose residents may have been affected by the shutdown — are preparing to challenge the declaration in court, according to The Associated Press.
While many Democrats have expressed opposition to a border wall, the issue has become somewhat politically complicated because of the broad popularity of physical barriers like fences. A recent Quinnipiac University poll found that nearly half of voters surveyed supported construction of a border wall, while 47 percent opposed it.

The Coalition of States consists of California, Colorado, Hawaii, Maine, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin. The plaintiffs filed suit in the Southern District of Arizona.

A new analysis released Tuesday shows that the wealthiest Americans benefited most from President Trump’s $1.5 trillion tax cut — particularly white men, who saw an average increase of $6,200 per household, compared with a national average of $1,120. That’s the latest piece of evidence that the tax code favors the richest families.
“Wealth is concentrating at the top again because of what’s happening to taxes,” says Roberton Williams, senior fellow at the Tax Policy Center and a co-author of the report. “It’s not that the rich are getting richer; it’s that everyone else is falling further behind.”
White women made more than twice as much under the new tax regime, gaining $1,500 per household, while Latinos and Asian-American households gained $1,000 each. Black Americans lost ground the most, earning about $400 less per household under the new tax system.
The overall benefits of the tax cut are inflated by how much it helps the upper class, economists say. Families making between $75,000 and $100,000 gained an average of $820, while those earning between $50,000 and $75,000 received a $620 average windfall. On the opposite end of the scale, low-income families didn’t see any noticeable gains from the cuts. Households earning less than $25,000 actually got worse off after the changes took effect, with an average decrease of $2,300 per household.
“If you look at the distribution of the total income of the population, almost all of the benefits of the tax law accrue to high-income families and the lowest 40 percent of the population have lower incomes,” says Williams. “There’s no doubt about it that there is huge unfairness built into the tax system. But I think even if you got rid of the whole thing, we wouldn’t eliminate it, because the structure is just so skewed towards the richest Americans. The fact that we are reducing some of the benefits for the rich doesn’t change the basic problem of the way the tax code is structured.”

At the time, only one candidate had a paid staffer focused entirely on social media. Now, every single major statewide contest has candidates with professional staff dedicated to tweeting and Facebooking. Here's some insight into why and what the effect of these social media operations might look like in 2020.
How do politicians use Twitter and Facebook?
Both of the major parties have their own headquarters in Washington D.C., where there are entire departments devoted to digital engagement. On the right, there is the National Republican Congressional Committee; on the left, there is the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Both of these organizations employ armies of young professionals to reach supporters through the latest forms of communication technology.
Twitter and Facebook are two major ways that candidates communicate directly with their audiences online. Some of these candidates even have entire staff members dedicated solely to using social media to spread information about events, press releases and other content. These individuals have come to be known as social media directors or digital strategists.
What does that mean for the candidates themselves?
It means that politicians can reach thousands — sometimes millions! — of voters instantly through social media. It doesn’t matter whether you’re running in a city, suburb or rural area: It’s now easier than ever to get your message out far beyond the local level. Candidates without the resources to buy television or radio spots can still get their names and causes before the eyes of large numbers of prospective voters.
But beware: There is an enormous amount of pressure for candidates to post the most interesting, exciting, shareable and retweetable content they can find. The challenge is finding it, organizing it and presenting it in a compelling way. But that’s no longer the difficult part. Now, all kinds of news outlets, interest groups, campaigns and even political consultants are making content for you! You simply need to find a way to filter the noise and determine what’s useful.

Election Day holiday: Election Day would become a national holiday, giving citizens the option of having a day off work or school if they do not wish to vote early.
National popular vote: A provision requiring electoral votes to be awarded to presidential candidates based solely on popular vote totals would go into effect once enough states (starting at 15) sign on. However, there is no time limit set for the number of states that must agree to the compact.
Police body cameras: Funds would be directed toward programs that distribute police body cameras, especially those involving departments with histories of brutality and excessive force.
Provisions that impact campaign finance include:
Disclosure of donations by corporations: Corporations would be required to disclose all of their political spending and activity.
Public financing of elections: Candidates would receive federal matching grants for voluntary contributions that go toward paying for campaigns. Candidates receiving 60% of their total contributions in increments of $200 or less could qualify for the funds. Matching funds would be available only through the general election portion of the campaign cycle.
Super PAC limits: Super PACs would be prohibited from raising more than $5 million per year; the overall cap on donations to super PACs would be reduced to $10 million. Additionally, super PACs would be barred from using money from the candidate’s campaign account.
Establishment of a new regulatory authority: A new Independent Federal Election Commission would replace the existing Federal Election Commission, which consists of five bipartisan commissioners who regulate campaign finance activity. The IFC would have four members appointed by the president — two Democrats and two Republicans — who would serve alongside six nonpartisan administrative judges.

Title: Donald Trump Vows To End Birthright Citizenship
Summary:
In a wide-ranging interview with news organization Axios that aired Sunday evening, President Donald Trump said he may sign an executive order terminating the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship for anyone born on American soil, including the children of noncitizens.
Background: According to the Fourteenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, "all persons born . . . in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens of the United States." The provision was enacted in response to concerns among Reconstruction-era leaders over slavery's legacy—including the lack of representation in Congress and other federal institutions for newly freed slaves. To assuage those concerns, the Fourteenth Amendment extended citizenship to African-Americans and provided a pathway for their political participation.
However, the text of the Fourteenth Amendment is ambiguous about whether children born to noncitizen mothers are entitled to citizenship, a point of contention since the first U.S. congressional debate over the provision in February 1869. While one faction argued that the amendment should guarantee the "absolute rights" of citizenship to all people born within U.S. borders, another maintained that Congress had discretion to regulate who could access those benefits. In the 1898 case U.S. v. Wong Kim Ark, the Supreme Court sided with the latter view, ruling that citizenship eligibility did not automatically extend to the children of "subject" individuals born in the United States. The court held, however, that such individuals were not excluded from naturalization proceedings.
Though critics have long derided the birthright citizenship provision, no president has attempted to curtail it until now. Trump's reported intentions follow months of speculation that he might use the constitutionally dubious strategy to fulfill his electoral promise of reducing immigration without having to go through Congress. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) called upon the president to declare a "national emergency" and invoke Section 287(g) of Title 8 of the U.S. Code to suspend birthright citizenship, although Graham himself admitted that he did not believe Trump actually possessed such power. The Trump administration announced Wednesday new restrictions on travel from Venezuela designed to further cut off the South American nation’s government following months of deadlock between U.S.-backed opposition leader Juan Guaido and embattled socialist President Nicolas Maduro.
The measures require Americans seeking a visa for travel to Venezuela to apply online, rather than at a consulate in person. They will also require any U.S. citizens leaving the country to sign an attestation confirming they received all of their vaccinations while in Venezuela. The measures will go into effect Thursday.
Trump administration officials also told HuffPost that they would begin restricting Venezuelan passport holders from entering the United States or receiving immigration benefits unless they first obtain a waiver. That move is likely to cause more chaos at border crossings amid the already fraught political and humanitarian crisis in the country.

Maduro has defied the Trump administration’s calls for his ouster and instead lashed out at the U.S., which he accused of orchestrating an assassination plot and stealing Venezuela’s assets. Last week, the socialist leader held what he billed as a “national dialogue” in Caracas where he sought to project an image of unity among key political actors in the country. But the process appeared to founder when Guaido sent his foreign minister to the meeting and then pulled out, citing concerns about the event’s legitimacy. Maduro was quick to pounce, announcing plans to form his own panel of international mediators, without mentioning Guaido, and to withdraw from any future talks sponsored by the European Union or Norway.
Guaido, meanwhile, returned home to Caracas on Monday after a six-day tour through Latin America and Europe during which he lobbied for greater economic penalties against the Maduro regime. Eligible immigrants may apply for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP, once they arrive in the country through the process called admission.

Qualifying immigrants must show proof of identity and age. Immigrants who are older than 60 and have a limited income are automatically eligible for SNAP, according to the USDA.

Legal permanent residents can get SNAP if they meet the income requirements of their state and live in the country legally. Most other immigrants are not eligible unless meeting certain requirements. The federal government determines an immigrant's residency status and how long it will last.
Immigrants may apply online or in person at local offices. Information needed includes date of entry into the country, immigration status, address and age information for each member of the household. Other requirements include having a bank account for direct deposit of benefits and providing Social Security numbers for each member. Summary: On Feb. 28, 2011, the U.S. Supreme Court heard oral argument in Comcast Corp. v. Behrend, a case in which the question was whether a federal district judge abused his discretion in certifying class members for antitrust purposes when he found that a methodological model used to determine damages was reliable and appropriate under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (FRCP) 23(b)(3). In a per curiam opinion, the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit’s ruling upholding the order granting class certification. Specifically, the Court held that district courts cannot certify classes before establishing that proposed classes are ascertainable. According to the Court, FRCP 23(c)(2), requires the trier of fact to use “appropriate” methods that are “reliable,” “economical,” and “not unnecessarily disruptive.” Additionally, the class representatives must “show that determining whether the representative party was injured is feasible.” However, given the lack of concrete guidance on how to achieve these conditions, the Court expressly noted that it may provide further clarifications on the ascertainability requirement through later cases.

Title: Supreme Court Hears Argument In Wal-Mart Sex Bias Lawsuit
Summary:
The US Supreme Court heard arguments today in Wal-Mart v. Dukes regarding the certification of a class action. A majority of the Justices questioned whether the class of over one million current and former female employees was ascertainable or too broad. They also expressed doubts about whether there was any uniform company-wide policy that applied equally to all women and whether there was any commonality of experience.
Lead counsel for the plaintiff class, Mr. Joseph M. Sellers, stated that a company-wide policy against gender discrimination could apply in every state and store owned and operated by Wal-Mart. However, Justice Scalia noted that the size of the class exceeded 1% of the population of the United States. In response, Mr. Sellers said that a company-wide policy could be challenged at the outset of the litigation or later when proof showed that a particular female employee in a particular position did not receive equal consideration based on gender.
At the outset, Chief Justice Roberts remarked that the parties agreed that each of the roughly one thousand store managers employed by Wal-Mart would have to be considered individually. Accordingly, the class consisted of roughly four hundred thousand current and former female store managers. Justice Alito noted that the class contained no individuals who either were never a manager or were never a woman. As such, he said the class was not ascertainable, which might be sufficient for denial of class status.
Justice Sotomayor observed that the Court should determine whether an individual store manager could be compared on the basis of gender in each state and/or district. She noted that a woman from the southwestern United States might have a very different experience from a woman in the northeastern United States. On the other hand, she indicated that the fact that the class contained more than one percent of the entire national population meant nothing.
Justice Kennedy wondered aloud whether the class could encompass all female hourly associates employed by Wal-Mart without defining a gender-neutral class consisting of all hourly associates regardless of their sex. Moreover, he thought it unlikely that the class was defined to include only females employed in similar positions throughout the country.
Justice Kagan questioned whether Wal-Mart could show that it had some uniform policies in place. Even if it did, she asked whether the employees’ experiences varied enough on the bases of location and position.

Title: AARP Pushes Back on Claim About Social Security Concessions as Lawmakers Push Reform
Summary:
The American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) says it is prepared to negotiate with Congress over reforms to the federal government’s main social insurance program—Social Security. The group had previously ruled out such discussions.
Background: Earlier this month, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released an update to its March report on the financial outlook for Social Security, projecting that the program’s trust fund would be depleted in 2033. In response, Treasury Department officials announced that they may act to borrow from the general treasury if interest rates rise and the need for funds becomes urgent. Such a move could increase risk to other programs, including mandatory spending. Last week, Senator Kay Bailey Hutchinson (R-TX) introduced legislation to address Social Security’s financial challenges without imposing higher tax burdens on current workers. Under the bill, Social Security’s Old Age, Survivors and Disability Insurance trust funds would receive immediate infusions of revenue through expansions of the employee payroll tax and employer contributions. The additional revenue would help rebuild the trust funds while also increasing payroll tax collections beyond those needed to meet scheduled benefits. The legislation would also require the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to conduct annual reviews of Social Security’s finances to ensure that funds are being spent wisely. The bill further directs the GAO to study the feasibility of establishing a Social Security Trust Advisory Board, consisting of experts appointed by the President. To mitigate risks from a decline in inflation, the bill prohibits the Social Security Administration from using price data produced by the Bureau of Labor Statistics or other agencies to calculate benefits. Finally, the measure would implement certain administrative reforms to reduce fraud, waste and abuse in the Social Security disability program.

Title: Justices Take Up Crucial Issue in Wal-Mart Suit
Summary:
Justices of the United States Supreme Court appeared divided on Tuesday (October 4th) on whether or not Wal-Mart should be able to sue the millions of female employees for allegedly discriminating against them based on gender. At first glance, this article appears to be about gender bias within Wal-Mart. Upon closer inspection, however, a clearer picture emerges. This article is really about the Supreme Court’s current interpretation of the law, specifically the precedent set by previous cases pertaining to class actions.
Analysis: When the Court ruled on the case Ricci v. DeStefano, in July of last year, it signaled that class actions could no longer be used simply to obtain monetary damages for a group of people without regard for what exactly made those people alike. To use the logic of Ricci, what if Wal-Mart, instead of being accused of discrimination, was accused of having poorly trained managers and was therefore unable to train and promote employees adequately? Would that case be classified as one of gender discrimination or lack of training? What is the Supreme Court’s role in such a situation? Who can decide what constitutes proper legal grounds for classifying a certain incident as one of gender discrimination? The Supreme Court’s role in the matter is to look at precedents regarding similar situations and determine how to apply the same criteria in new cases. If the judicial system is to become more efficient, then Supreme Court justices must have a better understanding of how society perceives these kinds of cases and how the general public will react to the judiciary’s rationale for making new rules.

Summary:
The Supreme Court heard oral argument yesterday in the massive sex-discrimination class-action suit brought against Wal-Mart by 1.5 million female employees. At stake is a ruling on whether the fact that hundreds of thousands of female employees had similar experiences at the world's largest private employer demonstrates sufficient "commonality" to bring a representative sample of these workers together in a single case. The plaintiff's counsel offered a combination of statistical analyses and testimony from a few named plaintiffs; the defense presented Wal-Mart's own data showing significant progress toward eliminating the pay gap. The justices focused their questions on the procedural hurdles involved in fashioning an effective remedy for the millions of female employees who lacked evidence that they had been discriminated against in pay or promotion decisions made at the local level. There was little optimism among either side that the case could be resolved without substantial disruption of business practices nationwide. Title: Justices Take Up Crucial Issue in Wal-Mart Suit
Summary: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in Wal-Mart Stores Inc. v. Dukes, No. 10-277, on April 24, 2011. During argument, the Justices considered questions relating to the applicability of the federal rule governing class actions (Rule 23) and the presumption of reasonableness underlying Rule 23(b)(2). Argument focused on the claims that Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (the Company) pays women employees less than men for substantially similar work, and whether the District Court erred in denying the Company's motion to dismiss the class action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), particularly on the ground that the named plaintiffs lacked standing as to the individual claims, or alternatively that the claims should be dismissed as a matter of law based on failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6). Argument also turned on the questions of whether the District Court properly certified the class of "all current and former female associates" in violation of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23 because the claims are inherently individual, and whether the District Court improperly certified the subclass of female employees within the class that seek backpay and compensatory damages instead of declaratory relief alone.

That means a person with an anxiety disorder should receive the same amount of medical care as someone with hypertension or high cholesterol. The argument that spouses should not be attacked is sound policy, but there are other factors that also help determine whether a candidate will get pushback. Here are three.
First, many political journalists are well aware that spouses play roles in politics. They know the role Heidi Cruz plays in her husband’s life. They may not care for her personally. But they do understand that the candidate who is married to her is a man who is likely to run a very different kind of campaign than the one being conducted now by Jeb Bush or Marco Rubio.
Second, when the candidates attack each other, it seems as though they are attacking their own families, too. There are many ways to insult a potential mate, but most of them are off limits during political season because of the way they can affect children, some of whom are also the targets of political attacks. So candidates often avoid them.
Finally, there is the way in which a candidate’s spouse appears in the public mind. As we move into the final stretch of the 2016 campaign, the view of the family lives of Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump will change. Many voters are still making up their minds about whether Mrs. Clinton can be trusted, given her history of scandals involving her use of a private email server while secretary of state. If Mrs. Clinton wins the Democratic nomination, it’s possible that her conduct could be used by Republicans as justification for rejecting her candidacy.

Summary:
As you can see, there really isn’t much news here (aside from some details on Obama’s actions and reactions). So I won’t try to summarize too much.
However, I feel like I must include this section because it says so much about the way CNN reports the news. Here is the first sentence in the introductory paragraph:
It took only hours for questions about those connections [between the shooter and ISIS] to become fodder in the presidential campaign.
First, look at the grammatical structure. Notice that this is an independent clause (a complete sentence) with a comma followed by the following two sentences. It almost sounds like this could be the beginning of a paragraph. However, these two sentences begin the second paragraph.
These are called parenthetical elements, and CNN likes to use these a lot. In fact, I think they write in a style that is almost entirely parenthetical elements. Take a look:
Hillary Clinton, the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, called the massacre in Orlando an “act of terror” and an “act of hate” and called for “hardening our defenses at home” while “refusing to be intimidated and staying true to our values” in the United States.
Notice that none of these four sentences includes a subject and predicate. Each contains two clauses, but these are not intended to form sentences. They are supposed to serve as short explanatory comments within the main body of the text.
So what does this mean? Well, it means that CNN journalists often leave out important information that would make their stories clearer, more coherent, and easier to understand. This is why I say they are writing in a style that is almost completely dependent upon parenthetical elements. This writing style can easily lead to confusion and misunderstandings.
I’ll have more on CNN’s writing style later…
