Title: Obama Will Meet With Sanders On Thursday
Summary: WASHINGTON -- With presumptive Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton officially reaching the number of delegates required for the nomination, President Barack Obama congratulated her on Tuesday evening, and signaled that the campaign of rival Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) might be coming to an end. According to the White House, Obama spoke to both Clinton and Sanders by phone following Tuesday’s primaries and caucuses and will meet with Sanders on Thursday, at Sanders’ request. “The President congratulated Secretary Clinton for securing the delegates necessary to clinch the Democratic Nomination for President,” White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest said in a statement. “Her historic campaign inspired millions and is an extension of her lifelong fight for middle-class families and children.” “The President thanked Senator Sanders for energizing millions of Americans with his commitment to issues like fighting economic inequality and special interests’ influence on our politics,” Earnest continued. Obama will meet with Sanders in Washington on Thursday, the same day the Vermont senator plans to hold a rally there. The meeting was arranged “at Senator Sanders’ request,” Earnest said, and the two will discuss “how to build on the extraordinary work he has done to engage millions of Democratic voters, and to build on that enthusiasm in the weeks and months ahead.” Obama has yet to make an endorsement in the race, but White House officials have said that it could come as early as this week. In recent months, Obama has privately suggested that Sanders drop out of the race to help Democrats unite around Clinton and prepare for the general election. He has also shown an eagerness to assail presumptive GOP nominee Donald Trump, which could be an important asset in helping Clinton defeat Trump in the general election.

Title: Clinton Is 'Sane' And 'Competent,' Unlike Trump, Bloomberg Tells U.S.
Summary:
There are many reasons why we cannot trust Donald Trump as president. This article offers two: He doesn't understand what he needs to know; and he has shown no inclination to learn anything at all.
Donald Trump may be the most ignorant man ever nominated by a major political party for President of the United States. When he first declared his candidacy last June, The Washington Post’s Philip Bump did some basic fact checking and quickly realized that Trump really wasn’t sure what being president even entails:
There are many things a president does not have control over — including how much money is spent on social programs, whether or not certain treaties go into force or whether there’s going to be a terrorist attack on U.S. soil. A president’s authority is limited by the Constitution and also by law.
And yet there was Trump, having just announced his candidacy, offering policy pronouncements on everything under the sun. That’s fine! said the press. Candidates always promise things they can never achieve, and voters know that. It’s just part of the game. But when reporters started asking him specific questions about issues in the news, they found that Trump either didn’t know the answer or — if he did — was unwilling to offer an honest response. As Bump recounts,
it quickly became clear that he was operating outside of the bounds of presidential expertise. His comments were frequently wrong, sometimes laughably so. They showed little awareness of history, economics and basic governmental processes.
He didn’t have to be able to name every Supreme Court justice in order to understand what the court does; he just needed to understand that the judiciary was an important branch of government whose decisions affect everyone in the country. He didn’t have to understand the details of military operations in Afghanistan; he just needed to understand that our troops had been in Afghanistan since shortly after Sept. 11 and that a strategy for ending the war there was essential.
Over the next few months, Trump continued to demonstrate that he knows very little about the inner workings of government.
These are only some of the many facts that Trump has gotten wrong, and you can find a lengthy list compiled by Media Matters here. In the process, he alienated lots of people who had previously considered voting for him and now see him as too big of a risk.

Title: Bloomberg says Trump a 'dangerous demagogue,' endorses Clinton at DNC
Summary:
At first glance, it looks like Mike Bloomberg's $75 million donation to the Democrats is going to pay off handsomely. Here's why it probably isn't...
The New York Times reported Thursday that former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg donated $75 million to the Democrats for the midterm elections. Bloomberg announced the gift Tuesday night during a fundraising dinner for House candidates in Los Angeles. It'll go toward ads by House Majority PAC, which backs Democrats, the Associated Press noted. But while the gift may appear to have been made to prop up the Democratic Party, it might actually prove counterproductive. The money will likely only embolden Republicans to fight harder than ever, and could also potentially make the Democratic Party even less attractive to moderates.
“You can bet your bottom dollar that every cent spent on attack ads against vulnerable House members by Democrats will now trigger a furious counterattack from the opposing side,” Larry Sabato, director of the University of Virginia Center for Politics, told Vox. “We haven’t seen the last of negative ads, but they should be somewhat diminished.”
Republican Rep. Dan Donovan (R-NY), whose bid for reelection could fall apart without such a boost from Bloomberg, welcomed the news. “New Yorkers will no longer be forced to underwrite national Democrats’ partisan attacks against their fellow citizens and neighbors,” he said in a statement. “It’s clear that some people have forgotten where their real loyalties lie.” And Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) released a video of himself celebrating the news.
Meanwhile, Bloomberg's contribution, especially because it came so late in the game, could discourage moderate Democrats from contributing to Democratic groups, who now know that major gifts will provide more bang for the buck than small contributions from individuals. That's already happening, reports the Washington Post:
Democratic committees and outside interest groups raised a combined $322.6 million through October, according to figures provided by the Center for Responsive Politics, a nonprofit group that tracks political spending. That’s more than twice as much as they raised during the same period
